Synchrotron X-ray Mapping of Xenon Sorption in Carbon Ink on Papyrus

Hannes Hoﬀmann, Tobias Arlt

1, André Hilger 1, Dirk Wallacher 1, Ingo Manke

1. Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin für Materialien und Energie, Institut für Elektrochemische Energiespeicherung,

Germany

Abstract

X-ray imaging of hidden carbon-based inks on organic substrates remains an unsolved problem

for the recovery of text from written artifacts. Collections that cannot be read without severe

textual fragmentation or physical destruction include the Herculaneum papyri and mummy

cartonnage, as well as isolated book scroll discoveries. Here, we propose the use of xenon

sorption in regions of increased carbon concentration to diﬀerentiate ink from substrate in the

X-ray imaging of these objects. A mock-up sample was placed in an aluminum vessel and exposed

to xenon atmospheres at pressures up to 10 bar. Using the BESSY II synchrotron light source, we

acquired a series of images to demonstrate the visibility of xenon uptake in ink particles as well

as its subsequent desorption from the sample.

Keywords

Xenon sorption, X-ray imaging, Carbon ink, Papyrus, Non-destructive analysis, Contrast agent,

Cultural heritage, Imaging contrast enhancement

Synchrotron X-ray Mapping of Xenon Sorption in Carbon Ink on Papyrus

Hannes Hoffmann ¹*, Tobias Arlt ², André Hilger ², Dirk Wallacher ², Ingo Manke ²

¹ Independent Researcher ² Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin für Materialien und Energie, Institut für Elektrochemische Energiespeicherung, Germany

* Corresponding author: hannes.hoffmann@gmail.com

Abstract

X-ray imaging of hidden carbon-based inks on organic substrates remains an unsolved problem for the recovery of text from written artifacts. Collections that cannot be read without severe textual fragmentation or physical destruction include the Herculaneum papyri and mummy cartonnage, as well as isolated book scroll discoveries. Here, we propose the use of xenon sorption in regions of increased carbon concentration to differentiate ink from substrate in the X-ray imaging of these objects. A mock-up sample was placed in an aluminum vessel and exposed to xenon atmospheres at pressures up to 10 bar. Using the BESSY II synchrotron light source, we acquired a series of images to demonstrate the visibility of xenon uptake in ink particles as well as its subsequent desorption from the sample. 1. Introduction Written artifacts from the ancient world are of great cultural significance. They promise direct insight into a lost world of ideas without the selection bias introduced by centuries of medieval recopying. Collections like the Herculaneum papyri, a group of mostly fragmentary carbonized scrolls of Epicurean literature, are expected to yield insights into ancient philosophy long lost from the literary corpus [1]. In Hellenistic Egypt, cartonnage was made from repurposed papyrus and animal glue. It was widely used in burial practice and mummy masks, with many of them encasing pieces of text. However, the practice of mechanical uncovering of written surfaces in scrolls or mummy cartonnage has caused the loss of such objects in the past. For the Herculaneum papyri in particular, destructive recovery methods left us with incomplete and discontinuous readings, which lead to irreversible losses and fragmentary text. Mechanical methods are largely seen as unacceptable today. X-ray-based methods have been applied to this problem, with mixed results. While some traces of heavy elements have been found in inks from the ancient world, they proved to be sporadic in concentration and occurrence [1,2]. Further, X-ray attenuation generally fails to differentiate carbon ink from organic writing substrates in the original papyri [3-5]. Texture based recognition of ink has been applied to very high-resolution X-ray images with limited success. Multiple lines of text have been recovered in one out of several scrolls. This demonstrates that

machine-learning-based image processing can be trained to recognize a structural pattern of the ink, if it occurs in tomography. However, as of the time of writing, any text accessible with this method remains highly fragmented and subject to speculative reconstruction [6]. We propose to use the concentration of carbon as a differentiator between ink and papyrus by leveraging the increased adsorption and absorption of xenon by this material. Ink pigments in the ancient world were primarily soot or various charcoals [7].While the papyrus substrate in some collections has seen some degree of carbonization as well, this is inconsistent. Some Herculaneum papyri display the characteristic reddish color of incomplete pyrolysis, and destructive experiments in the 18th Century found complex organics [8] In any event, the pigments have been intentionally and thoroughly carbonized before their and the papyrus’ joint encasement in volcanic mud. The ink binder, typically polysaccharides like gum arabic, is likely to turn into high grade charcoal due to compounding effects of volcanic heat, the presence of sulfuric acid, and 1700 years of deposit. While existing studies of Herculaneum papyri indicate all objects to differ in chemistry as well as microstructure, we assume an increase in carbon content and inner surface area to be a reliable feature of ink throughout the collection. We expect xenon to sorb in concentrated carbon more effectively than in plant material, and both

soot and charcoal to adsorb xenon well due to large surface values and resulting Van der Waals forces. Xenon, an inert noble gas, does not chemically react with the artifacts. With its high atomic number of 54, it acts as an excellent contrast agent in various imaging techniques, including attenuation micro-CT, dual-energy micro-CT, MRI and absorption edge synchrotron X-ray imaging [9], which is demonstrated here. Since an increase in attenuation contrast is beneficial for the effective resolution on X-ray imaging, texture-based ink recognition methods may see improvement by this method as well.

2. Materials To demonstrate an effective attenuation contrast in a material system of charcoal on papyrus, a mockup sample was produced from commercially available papyrus, high purity ‘medical’ charcoal powder and gum arabic in aqueous solution. It was overlaid with a frame-shaped piece of papyrus and a third layer of papyrus, creating a narrow space in the area where the ink was placed in the shape of a letter. It was then heated between two plates of aluminum until the characteristic reddish hue of incomplete endothermic pyrolysis appeared. The custom-made pressure vessel was machined from aluminum by the workshop at HZB and integrated into an experimental setup enabling controlled xenon gas delivery and pressure regulation (Fig.1, left)
Figure 1: Sample preparation and mounted sample housing on the piezo stage at BAMline. Red plastic tubes were used to fix the sample inside the housing.

Figure 2: Sketch of experimental plan. One energy below (green) and one energy above (blue) the Xe absorption edge was applied. The pressure of Xe atmosphere as stepwise increased from vacuum to 10 bar and back.

Figure 3: Cross-sections of absorption tomographic scans of same position inside the sample. The papyrus fragment can be seen in the middle part. Especially particles inside the ink are visible as bright areas, while the substrate fibers can hardly be identified. 3. Experiment The investigation on the sample was conducted on April 11, 2024, at the imaging beamline “BAMline” at the BESSY II synchrotron in Berlin, Germany [10]. The detector setup was set to a pixel size of 3.6 µm, using a pco edge 5.5 camera in combination with a 100 µm thick CdWO4 scintillator. To minimize the dose and scanning time to a suitable minimum, with respect to the SNR, 2000 projections and exposure time of 150 ms were chosen. Measurements were performed at energies of 33.3 keV and 34.9 keV under the varying pressure conditions of vacuum, 1 bar, 5 bar and 10 bar as shown in Fig.2. The sample was stabilized between tubes to minimize movement artifacts observed in prior setups using paper or Styrofoam. Xe-staining proved successful, rendering particles in the ink visible, although the geometry of these particles (<370 µm layer thickness, 10–150 µm particle size) would have been discernible even without Xe. Nevertheless, Xe enhanced contrast. Pressure variation in particular resulted in differential Xe distribution within the particles (Fig 3). Xe was detected in both the particles and the fiber structure. A significant portion desorbed after one hour under vacuum. Tomographic data revealed localized variations in Xe concentration, with diffusion effects observed: at 10 bar, accumulation began in parts of the

particles and progressed toward the center (Fig.6 and 7). Xe diffused out again after pressure release. One measurement was acquired immediately after the pressure release, followed by an additional measurement one hour later. The difference between the two measurements is shown in Fig. 4 and Fig. 5 Sample stability posed a challenge. Vibrations and pressure fluctuations (0–10 bar) caused sample movements that could only be corrected locally, e.g., using large particles as reference points. Global corrections were precluded by sample movement. The beam height limited measurements to a sample height of approximately 3 mm. Tomographic analysis revealed a weak Xe signal in the fibers, making them visible, while other regions remained difficult to identify. Difference images (e.g., 10 bar vs. vacuum, 34.9 keV vs. 33.3 keV) confirmed Xe presence in fibers and particles, with the latter appearing brighter due to stronger signals. Plots along selected lines demonstrated that Xe increased the attenuation coefficient, thereby improving contrast, though particles were detectable even without Xe. The findings suggest that Xe-staining is a valuable tool for contrast enhancement.
Figure 4: Sample environment: going from staining with Xe at 10 bar to vacuum condition. Tomography was taken directly after reaching vacuum condition
Figure 5: Sample environment: going from staining with Xe at 10 bar to vacuum condition. Tomography was taken 1h after reaching vacuum condition

Figure 6: Progression of staining on the same section shown as time series. Numbers refer to scan numbers as depicted in Figure 2. Result: different absorption and discharge times (presumably due to diffusion/adsorption) are marked by arrows

Figure 7: Analysis of the writings. A magnification of a cross-section though the ink layer is shown. Xe-related transmission changes, documented by a plot through a particle. Thickness of the writing was in the range of 20…370 µm 4. Discussion We successfully demonstrated, for the first time, the possibility of introducing effective attenuation contrast by xenon sorption into a material system of carbon ink on papyrus. Xenon is an excellent contrast medium. It may allow for the detection of ink in such systems by several modalities, including dual-energy micro-CT, Photon-counting m-CT and even possibly MRI. At relevant energy levels of less than 100 keV, its attenuation is about 18 times higher than that of iron ions, whose occasional presence in written artifacts has previously been used to image inaccessible writing [11, 5]. Desorption of xenon is seen within an hour of venting the xenon atmosphere. No change or damage to the material was observed. As an inert noble gas, xenon is not expected to chemically interact with the material in any way. It shares this feature with Helium, which is well proven as an atmosphere in the X-ray fluorescence analysis of fragile cultural objects. Noble gases differ in this regard from contrast agents like Iodine, which has been observed to persist in organic objects. Rapid uptake of xenon in some parts of ink particles followed by further absorption into the remaining regions seems to indicate an initial adsorption phase on high-surface-area particles, leading to absorption into the carbon volume. While the inner surface of ancient ink remains unpredictable, it can be assumed to be of higher carbon content, compared to the substrate. While efforts to image the collection from the Villa of the Papyri are ongoing, Herculaneum papyrology remains a jigsaw puzzle of disjointed text fragments. Recent efforts to use machine learning

for the recognition of texture [12] require very high resolutions and have so far only led to the recovery of some fragmented text [6]. An increase in attenuation could synergize with this method and improve noise-to-signal-ratios. Further, effective ink recognition could label the papyrus surfaces, allowing for machine-learning based segmentation of the distorted fragments and scrolls. To obtain continuous segments is a major problem in all imaging efforts of these objects so far. The apparent tendency of xenon to adhere to papyrus fibers and vascular bundles more than to other papyrus tissue holds promise for the reassembly of text in Herculaneum papyri. The vast majority of unrecovered text in this collection is to be found is fragments, many of which result from earlier efforts in physical unrolling. If letters in those fragments can not only be imaged but also linked with other physical fragments and text recovered in the unrolling efforts, continuous, meaningful readings may be achieved. With improved resolution of both fibers and vascular bundles in tomography, barcode-like sequences may be identified in the sheets and fragments may be matched. Both the improvements in ink recognition and fiber-‘barcoding’ may apply to cartonnage as well, therefore unlocking a whole class of artifacts for the non-destructive recovery of enclosed writing. We also note that some classes of fossils consist of small differences in texture and carbon concentration in material systems of low atomic numbers. Analog to papyri, carbonized fossils in limestone and from deposits like Burgess Shale or Messel may be imaged with improved contrast and detail if xenon sorption is applied.

5. Conclusion We have demonstrated that xenon sorption can effectively enhance the X-ray contrast of carbonbased inks on papyrus. The constituent particles exhibited varying degrees of xenon uptake, and no residual xenon was detected after desorption. This method, which employs xenon as an inert and nondestructive contrast agent, shows potential for the

recovery of inaccessible texts, such as the Herculaneum papyri. It may also support the matching of papyrus fragments based on fiber structure and could be extended to the imaging of other material systems with carbon differentials, including fossils.
